title: Shiva's third eye
hookLine: Shiva burns desire to ash with his third eye; what the mark on the forehead means
carry: a tilak marks the god you honor
last: EKADASHI IS A DAY GIVEN TO VISHNU.

cards: Shiva sits deep in meditation on his mountain, and the gods are desperate. A demon is ravaging the worlds, and only a son of Shiva can defeat him. But Shiva wants no wife and no son.
So the gods send Kama, the god of desire, with his bow of sugarcane and his arrows of flowers. Kama creeps close, draws, and lets an arrow fly. Shiva feels it.
And the eye in the middle of his forehead, his third eye, opens. Fire pours out, and Kama is burned to ash.

teach.h: THE THIRD EYE BURNS KAMA TO ASH.
teach.b: That's the Shiva Purana. Kama's wife Rati weeps, and he's allowed to live on, but without a body, which is why desire is everywhere and can't be seen. And Shiva is pictured smeared with ash.
Look at many devotees of Shiva today and you'll see that ash too: three lines of vibhuti, sacred ash, across the forehead.
That's a tilak, the mark on the forehead, and it's the teaching today: the tilak shows whom you honor.
It can be ash, cool sandalwood paste, or kumkum, a red powder made from turmeric.
The shape can tell you the lineage. Three lines of ash, for Shiva. A tall U or V, often with a line down the middle, for many devotees of Vishnu and Krishna.
A red dot, for many devotees of the Goddess, and others.

A bindi, from bindu, a point, is worn by many women and girls, and doesn't by itself mean someone is married; in many North Indian families it's sindoor in the hair parting that marks a married woman. Why the forehead?

teach.h: THE PLACE OF THE THIRD EYE.
teach.b: It's the place of Shiva's third eye, and in yoga texts a center called ajna, linked with insight. Many teachers read the mark as a reminder to see from there, with the eye that burned desire away.
And often it's given, not put on: by a priest after puja, or by an elder. So when a teammate asks about the smudge, there's a short, true answer.

teach.h: A TILAK MARKS THE GOD YOU HONOR.
teach.b: It's a tilak. It's a blessing, and it shows who I honor.

how: Many Hindus wear a tilak of kumkum, sandalwood paste or sacred ash, daily or after temple worship, its shape often showing their lineage; many women and girls wear a bindi, and in many North Indian families married women wear sindoor in the hair parting.

games.q: a coworker points at the red smudge on your forehead and asks what it is. what's a short, true answer?
o: it's a tilak, a blessing from the temple this morning.
games.why: a tilak is a mark of blessing and of what you honor; often a priest or an elder gives it.

practice: Close your eyes, breathe slowly, and without straining let your attention settle between your eyebrows, where a tilak would go, as if a cool fingertip of sandalwood were resting there; when the mind wanders, come back to that spot.
If you pray, you can hold there the form of God you honor. If you don't, simply look out from there for a while.

wordCard.voice: Tilak. The mark on the forehead: ash, sandalwood or red powder, worn as a blessing and a sign of the god you honor. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Hindi: a mark on the forehead, of ash, sandalwood or red powder.

carryVoice: Your line: a tilak marks the god you honor. Right where Shiva's third eye opens. Day one hundred thirty-one, and the week is done.
